item.title: Crude oil is trading lower after yesterday's run to the upside found willing sellers. What next?
item.description:
The rally stalled shy of the daily moving averages

Crude oil moved higher yesterday, reaching an intraday high of $87.38. That took the price back above the 50% midpoint of the move up from the July low at $86.86. The next two targets were the 200-day moving average at $87.89 and the 100-day moving average at $88.16. Both stayed out of reach, and the price slipped back below the midpoint into the close.

Sellers break the November low and eye $82.23

The downside momentum continued today, taking the price below the November 10 low at $83.88 and down to $82.38. That put crude within $0.15 of the 61.8% retracement at $82.23.

A move below $82.23 would increase the bearish bias and have traders looking toward the natural support at $80.00, followed by the August 26 low at $79.62.

The close barometer is $83.88

On the topside, a move back above $83.88 would give buyers a glimmer of hope. They would need to stay above that level to build confidence in a corrective move back toward the $86.86 midpoint. As long as the price stays below $83.88, the sellers hold the stronger hand.

In the video above, I walk through the failed move above the midpoint, why $83.88 is the closest barometer for bias and risk, and what a break below $82.23 would open up on the downside.

Meanwhile...EIA inventory data lean bearish for crude oil

US crude inventories rose by 3.380 million barrels, well above the 58,000-barrel build expected. Gasoline posted the biggest build and the biggest surprise, rising by 5.192 million barrels versus 1.645 million expected. Distillate stocks also rose more than forecast, up 1.571 million barrels versus 1.252 million expected.

The takeaway is bearish. Inventories built more than expected across crude, gasoline and distillates. The outsized gasoline build adds to the bearish bias from the crude headline and gives sellers another reason to lean against rallies.

Trading lesson. A break needs follow-through

The move above $86.86 gave buyers a technical victory. The next test was whether they could hold the midpoint on a pullback and build enough momentum to challenge the daily moving averages. Once the price fell back below $86.86, buyers lost the level they could lean against. The same test now applies at $83.88. If buyers reclaim it, watch what happens on the first pullback. A hold gives them a level to define their risk against, with $86.86 as the next upside target.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: US weekly crude oil inventories +3380K vs +58K expected
item.description:
• Prior was +4657K

  • Distillates +1571K vs +1252K exp

Private oil inventory data released late yesterday showed:

  • Crude +5300K
  • Gasoline +5100K
  • Distillates +400K

WTI crude oil was down $1.25 to $84.76 ahead of the report and extended losses by 50-cents afterwards.

For background, the US Energy Information Administration releases its Weekly Petroleum Status Report every Wednesday at 10:30 am ET, or Thursday in holiday-shortened weeks. Covering the week that ended the prior Friday, it’s the most closely watched regular data point for the oil market and one of the few energy reports that reliably moves crude prices.

The headline number is the weekly change in US commercial crude inventories, excluding the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Markets measure it against analyst estimates, with bigger-than-expected builds generally weighing on prices and surprise draws supporting them. Inventories at Cushing, Oklahoma, the delivery point for the WTI futures contract, get separate scrutiny because tight stocks there can squeeze the front of the futures curve.

The report goes well beyond crude. It tracks gasoline and distillate stockpiles, refinery throughput and utilization rates, domestic crude production, and imports and exports. Product supplied, a proxy for demand, shows how much gasoline, diesel, jet fuel and other products are moving into the market. Changes in the SPR are listed separately, since they reflect government purchases or releases rather than commercial supply and demand.

Weekly swings can be large and misleading. A delayed tanker or a shift in export timing can produce a multimillion-barrel build or draw that reverses the next week, and production figures are estimates rather than direct counts. Traders tend to weigh the combined change in crude and products, compare stocks with seasonal norms and focus on multi-week trends.

The American Petroleum Institute’s private survey, released Tuesdays at 4:30 pm ET, offers an early preview. The two reports often disagree, but the EIA figures are the official benchmark and usually set the tone for crude trading.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: US October pending home sales -4.7% vs -2.0% expected
item.description:
• Prior was -7.3% (revised to -7.2%)
  • Sales down 16.7% from October 2025

That 16.7% number is awful and highlights how the pricing in the market is hanging by a thread. It won't get any easier in the months ahead if the Fed keeps hiking either. Today Waller renewed his call for 50 basis points.

“October could mark the low point in contract signings for this housing cycle, as mortgage rates appear to have topped out,” said NAR Chief Economist Dr. Lawrence Yun.

“Two consecutive months of record-low pending contracts point to very sluggish fourth-quarter home sales closings, and annual existing-home sales could be the lowest since the mid-1990s,” Yun added. “It is somewhat puzzling that home sales would fall to levels last seen three decades ago, even as the U.S. population has grown by roughly 75 million. Either sizable housing demand is building in the background, or the dream of homeownership is increasingly out of reach for many Americans.”

For background, the National Association of Realtors publishes its Pending Home Sales Index monthly at 10 am ET, usually near the end of the month. It tracks signed contracts to buy existing homes, including single-family homes, condos and co-ops, making it the most forward-looking piece of NAR’s monthly housing data.

The index is benchmarked so that 100 equals the average level of contract activity in 2001, a year NAR considers a normal, balanced market. Readings are seasonally adjusted and reported as monthly and year-over-year changes. Results are also broken down by region: Northeast, Midwest, South and West.

Because a home sale typically closes one to two months after a contract is signed, pending sales lead NAR’s existing home sales report, which counts completed closings. Economists use the index to gauge where existing home sales are headed. The relationship isn’t perfect. Some contracts fall through because of financing problems, failed inspections or appraisal gaps, and cancellation rates can rise when mortgage rates jump or buyers get cold feet.

Contract signings are highly sensitive to mortgage rates, so the index often responds quickly to moves in Treasury yields. A drop in rates can show up in pending sales within weeks, well before it appears in closings or prices.

The report rarely moves broader markets, but it’s watched closely by homebuilder and mortgage-related stocks and as an early read on housing demand. In recent years, the index has hovered near historically low levels as high mortgage rates, stretched affordability and the lock-in effect, where homeowners are reluctant to give up low-rate mortgages, have kept buyers and sellers on the sidelines.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: As Bitcoin consolidates, the technical resistance gets closer and closer to the price. What next?
item.description:
Bitcoin continues to consolidate in a modest range, allowing the falling 100 hour moving average to catch up to the price. When Bitcoin reached its Sunday low at $61,947, the 100 hour moving average was up at $70,244 (close to $8300 above the price). Today, the moving average is down to $64,717, while Bitcoin is trading at $63,886. At today’s session high, the price nearly reached (i.e. was identical) the moving average before rotating back to the downside. That is as a result of the consolidation or breather, that the market is doing at the lower levels.  

In the video above, I take a look at the technicals, explain why traders are leaning against the 100 hour moving average, and outline the targets on a break in either direction.

The 100 hour moving average is the barometer

The last three tests of the 100 hour moving average have found willing sellers. That tells me traders are watching the level and using it to define their risk. As long as the price stays below it, the sellers remain in control.

If buyers can get and stay above $64,717, they would score a technical victory and have a level to lean against on a pullback. That would shift the short-term bias modestly to the upside. The next test would be whether buyers can build on the break and take out Sunday’s corrective high.

What are the targets on a break?

On the topside, a move above the 100 hour moving average at $64,717 would have traders looking toward Sunday’s corrective high at $66,069. Get above that level and the next targets come in at the falling 200 hour moving average at $68,203, followed by the broken 38.2% retracement of the November trading range at $69,265.

On the downside, the first support is near today’s lows around $63,800. A break below would put Sunday’s low at $61,947 back in focus. Below that, traders would look toward the natural support at $60,000, followed by the June low and the low for the year at $57,735.

The trading lesson

Consolidation can bring a falling moving average back into play even when the price makes little headway. On Sunday, Bitcoin was $8,297 below its 100 hour moving average. Today, it came close enough for sellers to lean against it again. If buyers finally get above it, watch what happens on the next dip. If the moving average starts to hold as support, buyers have a level to define their risk and a better shot at testing $66,069.

item.title: Macro signals from today's earnings: Target, TJX and Lowe’s
item.description:
Eyes are on the US consumer this week and yesterday's Home Depot numbers and government retail sales data were solid. Today it's more of the same with Target, TJX and Lowe’s reports pointing the same way. Spending is holding up better than expected. For this trio, it was coming from more shoppers rather than higher prices while big-ticket spending tied to housing is still weak.

Target (the strongest macro read):

  • This was Target’s best sales growth in five years. Comps rose 5.6% against 3.8% expected, driven by a 5% jump in traffic, while the average ticket rose just 0.6%. That’s an excellent signal on a broadening of volume, and not price hikes.
  • CEO Fiddelke said "It’s not just one consumer... The broad-based nature — by geography, by guest demographic, by income level — gives us confidence”. 
  • Target cited U.S. shoppers’ worries about the economy and their own finances as a reason it promoted price cuts this year, and cut prices on nearly 2,000 more items in the third quarter and is promoting sub $20 Christmas gifts. Apparel and home are still weak, and a year ago comps were -2.7%, so the comp was easy.

TJX (Canada strong)

  • Comparable sales rose 4% against a 2–3% guide. Somewhat worrisome was that the US was +2%, versus +6% a year earlier. HomeGoods was +5%, Canada +6% and International +8%
  • Q4 comps are guided to +2–3%. The full-year comp was raised to 4% from 3% to 4%.
  • Strip out tariff refunds and gross margin fell 0.5 pts on freight and fuel. Adjusted pretax margin slipped 0.2 pts to 12.5%.
  • Management called merchandise availability “outstanding.” That’s code for other retailers sitting on excess goods, which is disinflationary for apparel and home.

Lowe’s (housing still stuck)

  • Comparable sales rose 1.8%, above the 0.4% consensus, driven by a 17.4% increase in online sales and solid sales to professional customers and home services
  • The full-year comp moved up to about +0.5% from flat, but operating margin guidance slipped to about 11.1% from 11.2%.
  • CEO Ellison told CNBC Lowe’s “can grow” despite economic headwinds and a sluggish housing market. He had previously told CNBC he expects consumers to remain cautious through the end of the year
  • Gross margin fell 124 bps to 32.95% even with ~$250m in tariff refunds. That implies an underlying hit of more than 2 pts

At last check, here were the pre-market changes in the trio: 

  • TGT +0.3%
  • TJX +5.9%
  • LOW -5.6%

You can see the market had built in beats on comp sales, which is part of the usual sandbagging. From a purely macro perspective though, the signals were solid, particularly from Target. There is no sign the consumer is meaningfully weakening, though Christmas is the big test.

We get Walmart earnings tomorrow and that's the strongest macro view you will get from a retailer. S&P 500 futures are up 0.35% but that's all about Nvidia.

item.title: US October housing starts 1.309M vs 1.245M expected
item.description:
• Prior was 1.221M
  • Starts change +9.9% vs -5.2% prior
  • Building permits 1.295M vs 1.377M expected
  • Prior permits 1.398M
  • Permits change -7.4% m/m vs vs -0.4% prior

This is a rare win in US housing data and runs counter to rising mortgage rates and a long string of poor reports, including rock-bottom homebuilder sentiment. I would take it as a one-off until further notice, particularly with the fall in forward-looking permits.

For background, the US Census Bureau and the Department of Housing and Urban Development publish the New Residential Construction report monthly at 8:30 am ET, usually in the third week of the month. It’s released the day after the NAHB homebuilder sentiment index and offers the first hard data on new home construction each month.

The headline figure is housing starts, the number of new privately owned homes on which construction began, reported as a seasonally adjusted annualized rate. The report also includes building permits, which are issued before construction begins and are generally viewed as a better leading indicator of future activity. It also covers completions, homes authorized but not yet started, and units under construction.

Starts and permits are split between single-family homes and buildings with five or more units. The multifamily category is highly volatile because a handful of large apartment projects can swing the monthly figure, so markets tend to focus on single-family starts and permits for the underlying trend. Results are also broken down by region: Northeast, Midwest, South and West.

The monthly data have wide margins of error, and changes in a single month are frequently not statistically significant. Revisions can be large, which is why economists tend to look at three-month averages.

Housing starts feed into residential investment, a component of GDP that’s highly sensitive to interest rates and often leads the broader business cycle. The report rarely moves markets dramatically, but it shapes the outlook for homebuilders and suppliers. Mortgage rates, affordability, construction costs, tariffs on building materials and labor availability are the main forces driving the data.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Why earnings reports rarely change the bigger picture: the macro environment matters more
item.description:
Every earnings season brings a fresh wave of volatility. Companies report their quarterly results, investors reassess valuations, analysts adjust their forecasts and individual stocks can move dramatically in either direction.

Earnings reports can certainly move individual stocks, but they rarely change the broader economic and financial conditions that ultimately determine the direction of the stock market. Earnings tell you what happened in the past, while markets are constantly trying to price what might happen in the future.

Stanley Druckenmiller once said that earnings don't move the overall market; the Federal Reserve does. He suggested that investors should focus on central banks and liquidity rather than conventional measures such as earnings.

Monetary policy influences the discount rate applied to future cash flows, borrowing costs and overall financial conditions. When interest rates rise and liquidity becomes tighter, equity valuations can come under pressure even if corporate earnings remain strong. The opposite is also true. When monetary policy becomes more accommodative, real yields decline and financial conditions ease, investors may become willing to pay higher multiples for future earnings.

In other words, the same earnings outlook can justify very different stock market valuations depending on the prevailing economic context. This is why the economic cycle matters so much. Strong corporate earnings cannot indefinitely offset an increasingly restrictive monetary environment or a deteriorating growth outlook.

Companies' forward guidance

One could argue that forward guidance provided by companies solves the backward-looking problem because it provides an indication of what management expects in the coming quarters. However, even forward guidance needs to be treated with caution.

Companies have incentives to manage market expectations. Some communicate ambitious growth targets to reinforce investors' confidence, while others may adopt conservative guidance that leaves room for earnings beats.

Mmanagement forecasts are not independent or objective assessments of future economic conditions. An extarnal shock can change future expectations on a dime, and the stock market will immediately reflect that change. 

Take Oracle for example. In September 2025, Oracle shares surged roughly 43% to a record high after the company announced several multibillion-dollar AI cloud contracts and delivered an extremely optimistic long-term revenue outlook. Management projected Oracle Cloud Infrastructure revenue would grow from $18 billion in the current fiscal year to $144 billion by fiscal 2030.

However, that rally ultimately marked the top. Oracle eventually experienced a massive decline, with shares falling roughly 67% from their September 2025 peak. 

Good earnings don't guarantee a rally

Nvidia provides another example of why good earnings and forward guidance do not guarantee a rally. If you look at recent earnings reports, the stock has certainly experienced volatility. Strong earnings and optimistic guidance have often generated an initial buying wave, but those gains have rarely resulted in a sustained rally.

In most cases, the stock erased its post-earnings gains or even fell below the pre-earnings levels. For example, Nvidia declined following its May 2026 earnings report despite beating revenue and earnings estimates and providing strong forward guidance. The stock experienced a similar pattern following the previous reports.

There have been periods when strong earnings and guidance triggered sustained rallies, however the economic context was also positive in those instances.

Traders should focus instead on the macroeconomic environment, market positioning and expectations. A very dovish Federal Reserve will almost always result in a bullish stock market, even in the presence of disappointing earnings. Overcrowded markets are also very dangerous when the macroeconomic conditions start pointing towards an economic slowdown. 

Markets are forward-looking and they constantly price and reprice expectations about the next say 6–12 months. Quarterly earnings show how a company has performed in the past, not how it's going to perform in the future. The key is to focus on what the economic environment implies for future earnings.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Fed's Waller calls for more aggressive action to break psychology that 3% inflation is the norm
item.description:
Fed Governor Waller is becoming increasingly concerned about the US inflation outlook, warning that price pressures are broadening beyond energy and that the Fed risks allowing higher inflation to become entrenched in consumers' and businesses' expectations.

Waller argues that the central bank needs to take a more aggressive action to convince markets and the public that it remains committed to bringing inflation back to its 2% target.

He highlighted that roughly 70% of components in the core services basket are currently experiencing inflation above 3%, suggesting that price pressures are no longer concentrated in energy-related categories.

He is concerned that businesses are becoming comfortable passing higher prices on to consumers, partly because they believe consumers remain resilient enough to absorb those increases.

If businesses expect to raise prices and consumers increasingly accept 3% inflation as normal, inflation expectations could become more entrenched, making it harder for the Fed to bring inflation back down, without a more aggressive tightening.

He thinks the Fed needs to break the psychology that inflation around 3% has become the new norm after failing to bring it back to the 2% target since 2021. He stressed that the Fed needs to become more aggressive, either by delivering a 50 bps rate hike or use monetary policy communications to signal a significantly tougher stance in the months ahead.

Simply maintaining the current policy trajectory might not be enough to change inflation expectations. The Fed needs to convince businesses, consumers and financial markets that it is prepared to take stronger action to restore price stability. He even suggested that the central bank might need to go beyond reversing the rate cuts implemented last year to bring inflation under control.

He also argued that the Fed should use statements, press conferences and forward guidance to steer market expectations towards a more restrictive policy outlook. A hawkish communication strategy could push interest rate expectations higher and tightening financial conditions enough to weigh on economic activity and inflation.

He also questioned the usefulness of the December Summary of Economic Projections (SEP), arguing that year-end projections might not adequately capture the evolving inflation picture. He prefers adopting a more forceful and forward-looking communication strategy rather than relying too heavily on projections that could quickly become outdated.

For now, Waller remains the only governor suggesting a more aggressive action, with the majority of Fed members preferring to move in small steps. Nevertheless, he's been a very influential member and his views have always preceded a change in monetary policy since 2021. 

In the current context, traders should be very careful buying risk assets unless the Iran war ends or the Fed turns surprisingly dovish. 

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: Nasdaq analysis after the much anticipated Nvidia earnings
item.description:
Nasdaq futures after Nvidia: The rebound has more volume. Can buyers make it count?

Market analysis and trading education | November 18, 2026

Nasdaq-100 futures traded 35% more contracts than their recent European-morning average following Nvidia's earnings. But higher trading activity has not produced a convincing breakout, leaving traders with important price levels to watch.

Nasdaq-100 futures are recovering after Nvidia's latest earnings report, but is the rally running out of volume? The evidence suggests otherwise. Trading activity is above recent norms when we compare the same times of day. The bigger question is whether that increased activity can help buyers hold higher prices.

A trader on social media in the last hour made an interesting prediction: "I don't think Nasdaq is going to hold. We're going to finish red because the recent rallies lack volume." Perhaps the market will finish lower, perhaps it won't. But there is an important question worth asking before accepting that reasoning: Lack of volume compared with what?

Many traders look at volume bars and compare them with a moving average. That can be useful, but it can also be misleading. Trading activity naturally changes throughout the day, and a moving average may combine relatively quiet periods with unusually active ones. In this particular case, the average was influenced by elevated overnight trading following Nvidia's earnings. Comparing today's European morning with those unusually active hours is not necessarily comparing apples with apples.

A more meaningful approach is to compare the same time slots across different trading days. For example, the 11:00-11:30 Berlin time bar on November 18 recorded 5,027 Nasdaq futures contracts, approximately 20% below its 20-bar moving average. At first glance, that might suggest weak volume. But compared with the same half-hour across the previous six trading days, activity was actually 37% above average! Across the seven completed morning bars, total volume was approximately 35% higher than the comparable six-day average.

That gives us a very different interpretation of the same market. It doesn't guarantee the rally will continue, and the trader's bearish prediction could still prove correct. It simply means that the argument about weak volume is not supported by this more relevant comparison. The broader lesson is to understand what your indicator is measuring, choose an appropriate benchmark, and then examine whether price can actually hold important levels. Higher volume tells us there is more activity, not who will ultimately win the battle between buyers and sellers.

The Nasdaq recovery is more active than it first appears

Between 08:00 and 11:30 Berlin time on November 18, CME E-mini Nasdaq-100 futures (NQ) recorded 42,335 contracts across seven completed 30-minute periods.

That compares with 34,181 contracts during the same period on Tuesday and an average of approximately 31,375 contracts across the previous six trading days.

That represents 34.9% more trading volume than the recent six-day average, and the highest comparable morning total in this seven-session sample.

So why might a trader looking at a conventional volume indicator get the impression that trading activity is weak?

Consider the final completed 30-minute period, from 11:00 to 11:30 Berlin time.

It recorded 5,027 contracts, approximately 20% below its rolling 20-bar volume average of 6,310. However, compared with the same half-hour across the preceding six trading days, volume was actually 37% higher.

Both observations are correct, but they answer different questions.

The rolling average includes earlier, unusually active overnight trading following Nvidia's earnings. Comparing identical clock-time periods gives a more useful picture of whether this particular part of the session is unusually quiet or active.

This is an important trading lesson: volume should be evaluated in context, not in isolation.

Nvidia delivered strong earnings, but the price reaction tells a more complicated story

Nvidia reported third-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue of $115.8 billion on November 17, up 103% from a year earlier. The company also projected approximately $130 billion in revenue for the following quarter, plus or minus 3%.

Nasdaq futures initially reached 27,609.75 after the announcement, but failed to sustain trading above Tuesday's high of 27,498.

Prices subsequently retreated to 27,093 before recovering during the European morning.

By the 11:30 Berlin analysis cutoff, NQ stood at 27,365, above Tuesday's final recorded close of 27,126 but slightly below Wednesday's session opening level of 27,382.

This tells us something important. Higher trading volume has accompanied a recovery, but it has not yet established clear bullish control.

The market is still trying to decide how much of the initial post-earnings repricing it is prepared to maintain.

Nasdaq futures key levels: What traders should watch next

The following levels refer to E-mini Nasdaq-100 futures as of 11:30 Berlin time on November 18. They are not live quotes.

27,410-27,425: The immediate resistance test

This area includes a developing upper value-area boundary around 27,416 and two recent morning highs. Holding above it on completed candles, rather than briefly crossing it, would make the recovery more convincing.

27,485-27,500, followed by 27,610: The next upside obstacles

The first area includes Tuesday's high near 27,498. Above that, Wednesday's post-earnings high at 27,609.75 becomes an important test of whether buyers can regain the initial optimism.

27,260-27,320: A support area worth protecting

This region contains several estimated areas of previous trading interest, as well as the session's volume-weighted average price near 27,317 at the analysis cutoff.

Continued trading above this region would support the recovery argument. Falling back below it would suggest that buyers are giving up some of their morning progress.

27,093: The overnight low

If the recovery weakens materially, this is a significant lower reference. A sustained break would put Tuesday's low near 26,658.50 back into focus.

Volume-derived value boundaries are estimates and can change as the session develops.

A lesson for traders: Strong volume is not the same as strong price acceptance

Tuesday provided another useful example. An earlier Nasdaq futures rally attracted considerable trading activity but did not prevent a subsequent decline.

This is why volume alone cannot establish whether a rebound will succeed.

Traders should combine the amount of trading activity with what price actually achieves. Does it break resistance and stay above it? Does an earlier resistance area become support? Or does price repeatedly retreat despite higher trading activity?

For now, the constructive scenario would involve holding the nearby support region, sustaining trading above 27,425 and eventually challenging higher resistance.

Repeated rejection followed by a loss of 27,260-27,320 would weaken that interpretation.

There is also a third possibility: Nasdaq futures continue trading between these areas without establishing a clear direction. In that situation, waiting for better evidence may be more sensible than forcing a trade.

The first regular U.S. stock-market session following Nvidia's earnings, scheduled to open at 15:30 Berlin time, remained ahead at this analysis cutoff.

The takeaway: Nasdaq futures' European-morning rebound has attracted above-average volume. Whether that activity translates into lasting buying strength remains an open question. Price behavior around the next important levels will help traders judge the answer.

item.title: Gold analysis shows we may be in an interesting potential bottom zone
item.description:
Gold futures are showing signs of a possible bottom. Three price areas could decide what happens next

Gold buyers are finally showing some resistance after an extended decline. Improving price action near $3,766 and a recovery toward $3,780 offer encouraging clues, but a sustained move toward $3,800 may be needed before the recovery becomes more convincing.

Gold futures are beginning to show something that has been missing during much of their recent decline: selling pressure is no longer consistently producing lasting lower prices. Buyers have made some encouraging progress, but there is still a substantial difference between identifying a possible bottom and confirming a bullish reversal.

The latest intraday evidence provides a practical framework for evaluating that difference.

Market snapshot: November 18, 2026, approximately 4:29 a.m. US Eastern time. Analysis based on December 2026 Micro Gold futures (MGC), with gold near $3,780.60. All prices below refer to that observation, not continuously updated quotations.

What has changed in gold's price behavior?

Gold recovered from an observed intraday low near $3,759.50, climbing back into an important area where much of the session's trading activity had previously taken place.

The lower boundary of that developing value area was around $3,766.20.

For readers unfamiliar with volume-based analysis, a value area represents a range where a substantial portion of trading volume has occurred. Its boundaries can help traders assess whether the market is accepting or rejecting a particular price region.

Gold initially moved back above that boundary, briefly slipped beneath it again, and subsequently recovered.

What makes the sequence interesting is that buyers did not surrender all their progress during subsequent pullbacks.

Instead, the shorter-term price structure began retaining higher prices.

The recovery eventually extended toward $3,780, accompanied by improving buying participation and upward price progress.

This suggests sellers may be losing some of their earlier effectiveness.

However, stronger buying in a short-term recovery does not automatically mean the broader bearish trend has ended.

Gold futures key levels to watch

These are reference levels, not automatic buy or sell instructions. VWAP, its deviation bands and the developing value area can move as trading continues.

The $3,777-$3,780 area: Can buyers hold their recent gains?

At the latest observation, gold was trading above its first lower VWAP standard-deviation band, located around $3,777.60.

VWAP, or volume-weighted average price, measures the average traded price weighted by volume.

A market trading below VWAP has generally been transacting beneath that average. Recovering toward it can be meaningful, particularly after an extended period of weakness.

For the bullish case, maintaining prices around $3,777-$3,780 would be encouraging.

If pullbacks repeatedly find buyers around this region, the recovery could gradually become more convincing.

But what if gold briefly holds this area and subsequently falls back toward $3,766?

That would not automatically establish another bearish trend leg. It would mean traders need to reassess whether the market can defend its earlier recovery.

An important educational lesson is that support and resistance are areas to observe, not magical lines that guarantee a reaction.

Why the $3,800 area could become especially important

The developing VWAP was near $3,800-$3,801 during the observation.

This creates two potentially interesting situations, depending on whether a trader is already participating in the recovery or is still waiting.

For somebody who entered a long position at lower prices, approaching VWAP could provide an opportunity to consider taking partial profits.

That is not mandatory. It depends on the original entry, position size, risk and trading plan.

But reducing exposure near a potentially difficult resistance area can sometimes be a sensible way to manage an existing position.

For somebody who has not entered, the same area offers a different lesson.

Instead of chasing gold higher toward resistance, why not observe how buyers behave when they get there?

A brief move above VWAP would be encouraging, but a sustained move above it, followed by a successful retest, would offer stronger evidence that buyers are establishing control.

That could eventually bring the $3,816-$3,817 region into focus.

For now, it remains a conditional scenario rather than a forecast.

What would weaken the argument that gold is forming a bottom?

The developing value-area low, near $3,766.20, deserves particular attention.

If gold falls below this area temporarily and recovers, buyers may still have an opportunity to defend the developing structure.

However, repeated trading below it, failed attempts to reclaim it and renewed downward price progress would be much less encouraging.

A subsequent break beneath the observed $3,759.50 low would further weaken the case for a developing bottom.

The earlier lower reference near $3,755 could then become relevant, although there is no guarantee that it would provide support.

There is also a third possibility: gold might simply spend considerable time trading between roughly $3,766 and $3,800.

Not every attempted bottom leads immediately to a strong rally. Some fail, while others develop into lengthy periods of consolidation.

Waiting for clearer evidence can be a reasonable trading decision.

What the trading volume tells us about buyers and sellers

One useful lesson from the recent price action concerns the relationship between trading activity and actual price progress.

Earlier in the decline, aggressive selling frequently succeeded in pushing gold lower.

More recently, some selling attempts have produced less lasting downside progress.

At the same time, buying activity during the recovery has increasingly produced higher prices.

That relationship matters.

Heavy selling volume does not automatically mean a market must continue falling. If sellers remain aggressive but struggle to push prices lower, the balance between buyers and sellers may be changing.

Likewise, heavy buying volume is not necessarily bullish if prices fail to advance.

The important question is not simply how much buying or selling took place, but what that activity actually achieved.

The recent evidence is somewhat more favorable to buyers, but broader session participation has not yet provided an unambiguous bullish confirmation.

Gold traders also face a major Federal Reserve event today

The broader market environment remains challenging for gold.

A stronger US dollar, elevated Treasury yields and expectations of tighter Federal Reserve policy have contributed to the metal's recent weakness.

The Federal Reserve is scheduled to release minutes from its October 27-28 meeting on November 18 at 2:00 p.m. Eastern time.

A shift in interest-rate expectations could affect gold, the dollar and Treasury yields, potentially changing the short-term technical picture.

For traders, including those participating in prop-firm evaluations, this makes execution risk particularly relevant.

One Micro Gold futures contract represents 10 troy ounces. A hypothetical $14 adverse price movement therefore represents a $140 loss per contract before commissions and slippage.

That may be significant when compared with a trader's available risk allowance.

Traders should distinguish a promising market direction from a trade with an acceptable entry, stop distance and potential reward. Funded-account restrictions and drawdown rules also depend on the specific program.

For additional context, see investingLive's guide to leverage and margin risk.

The practical takeaway: Buyers have made progress, but the bigger test is ahead

Gold is beginning to offer bulls encouraging evidence that the recent selling pressure is becoming less effective.

Three areas provide a useful monitoring framework.

Above $3,777-$3,780: Watch whether gold retains the recovery and continues toward the developing VWAP.

Around $3,800-$3,801: Watch whether buyers encounter resistance or establish sustained trading above VWAP.

Back toward $3,766: Watch whether buyers can once again defend the developing value-area boundary. Acceptance below it would weaken the recovery case.

For longer-term investors, these intraday developments may be an interesting early clue, but they are not sufficient to confirm a major trend reversal. Stronger evidence across daily and weekly charts would still be valuable.

The market does not owe traders a clean bottom, an attractive entry or a profitable recovery.

Even a correct directional assessment can produce a losing trade if the entry, position size or risk management is unsuitable.

The more useful approach is to identify what would support the developing bullish interpretation, what would contradict it, and when patience might be preferable.

Gold buyers have made progress. Whether they can retain that progress is the next question.

What are FX option expiries?

The FX option expiration price levels refer to the strike prices where option contracts are set to expire. These levels include both calls and puts.

When you see "EUR/USD at 1.1600 for €4 billion" it means there is a total of €4 billion worth of options (calls + puts combined) that have a strike price of 1.1600 and are expiring at that specific time (the "New York Cut" at 10:00 AM ET).

Traders watch these levels because they often act as a "magnet" for the price. For example, if there's nothing happening in the market and the price is close to the expiry level, let's say 30-50 pips away, what you will usually see is the price moving into the expiry level. This happens due to the hedging activity of the market makers (banks, dealers and so on).

As the price gets closer to the strike price near expiration, these market makers must aggressively buy or sell the currency to hedge their risk. This hedging activity tends to suppress volatility and keep the price "pinned" close to the strike price until the expiration time passes.

  • Services CPI +3.7% vs +3.8% expected
  • Prior +3.7%
  • Full report

The market is focusing on the miss in services inflation and the unchanged core reading. The main upward pressure came from transport costs, particularly motor fuels, which made the largest positive contribution to the change in headline inflation. Restaurants and hotels provided the largest offsetting downward contribution.

The composition of inflation still warrants some caution, though. Goods inflation continued to accelerate, with the CPI goods annual rate rising from 3.2% to 3.5%. Services inflation, which is important for assessing domestic price pressures, remained relatively contained. 

Overall, the data will be welcomed by the Bank of England as stable core and services inflation provide some reassurance that underlying price pressures are not deteriorating significantly. This is leading to some minor dovish repricing and weighing on the British pound.

The probability for a rate hike in December fell to 78% from 89% before the CPI release. 

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

Nvidia and equities

item.title: Recap: Australian wages grow at fastest pace in nearly 3 years, yet swaps see a 75% RBA peak
item.description:
The Australian dollar barely moved, holding around 0.67, because traders treated the data as backward-looking and are focused on Thursday’s jobs report. Swaps still lean towards a peak in rates. A firm jobs number would challenge that, lifting front-end yields and supporting the currency, while a rise in unemployment would reinforce bets on easing by 2027. The contrast between strong wage growth and rising layoffs creates two-way risk for Australian bank stocks and rate-sensitive retailers, especially given the job cuts at David Jones and Bunnings. Watch the jobless rate on Thursday more closely than the headline jobs figure.

--- Australia now has wages, interest rates and unemployment all rising together, which leaves the RBA choosing between the pay data and the layoff headlines.

Summary:

  • The wage price index rose 1.1% q/q in Q3, the fastest since late 2023, ahead of forecasts of 0.9% to 1.0%
  • Annual growth was 3.5%, with the private sector at 3.4% and the public sector at 3.9%
  • The 4.75% award wage increase drove private pay, and rises for state frontline workers lifted public pay
  • Real wages fell 0.4% y/y, a fourth straight quarterly decline
  • Unemployment is at a five-year high of 4.7%, and David Jones and Bunnings are cutting jobs
  • Swaps imply about a 75% chance the RBA has peaked, ahead of Thursday’s jobs data

Australian wages grew at their fastest pace in nearly three years in the September quarter, giving the Reserve Bank of Australia more reason to keep policy tight even as cracks appear in the jobs market.

The Australian Bureau of Statistics said its wage price index rose 1.1% in the quarter, the strongest result since late 2023. That broke a run of five quarters at around 0.8% and topped forecasts of between 0.9% and 1.0%. Annual growth picked up to 3.5% from 3.2%. Private sector pay rose 3.4% over the year and public sector pay 3.9%, Reuters reported.

The ABS pointed to two drivers. The Fair Work Commission’s 4.75% increase in minimum and award wages from July lifted private sector pay, while raises for state government frontline workers pushed up public sector wages. Public sector pay has now outpaced the private sector for seven straight quarters. Real wages are still going backwards, down 0.4% over the year, the fourth consecutive quarter of decline.

For the RBA, the harder question is what it may take to bring inflation down. If pay keeps rising at this rate, the bank may have to tolerate a jobless rate higher than it currently projects, possibly above the level it regards as consistent with steady inflation. The central bank has argued that the labour market is easing, yet pay growth shows little sign of cooling broadly. And unless productivity picks up, wage gains of this size sit uneasily with inflation returning to the 2% to 3% band. For households, at least, bigger pay rises offer some relief after a long squeeze.

The bank lifted rates for a fifth time this year in November, to an 18-year high of 4.85%, partly because it judged the labour market to be a little tight. Three board members opposed the move, concerned the economy could be heading for a materially sharper downturn. One economist noted that Australia is in the unusual position of having unemployment, interest rates and wages all rising at once, and said wage growth and joblessness are likely to stay elevated through 2027.

There are signs that the labour market is weakening. Unemployment hit a five-year high of 4.7% in September, and layoffs are spreading. Department store David Jones plans to cut 1,500 jobs by the end of the year, and hardware chain Bunnings said this week it would cut around 230 permanent roles.

That puts Thursday’s employment report in focus. Forecasts point to a rise of 25,000 jobs in October and an unchanged unemployment rate of 4.7%.

Markets largely looked through the wage figures, treating them as backward-looking. Swaps still imply about a 75% chance that the RBA has finished raising rates, with roughly 20 basis points of easing priced by the end of 2027. A strong jobs report on Thursday would test that confidence, while a weak one would strengthen the case of the three dissenters.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold’s worst enemy right now is a 5% Treasury yield, not the headlines from the Middle East
item.description:
A break below $3,800 removes a key psychological level and leaves gold exposed to further selling if the Fed minutes sound hawkish. Gold miners and silver are likely to stay under pressure, though silver has been holding up better in recent sessions. For traders, gold is now trading as a rates instrument: US yields and Fed pricing matter more than geopolitical headlines. A spike in oil prices from the Iran war would likely add to the pressure by lifting inflation expectations and Fed hike bets. Any dovish surprise from the Fed would be the main trigger for a short-covering bounce.

--

Earlier:

  • Goldman’s second gold forecast downgrade in a month turns its bear case into the base case

--

A year ago gold was rallying on hopes of Fed cuts. Today it is under $3,800 because the Fed is hiking, and even the Iran war is working against it.

Summary:

  • Spot gold fell about 1.4% to around $3,795, its lowest in more than a year, and futures fell almost 1.8%
  • Markets price about a 96% chance of a December Fed hike, with a small chance of 50bp
  • US 10-year yields are near 5.1%, and the dollar is near a 19-month high
  • A year ago gold was rallying on expectations of two or three Fed cuts in 2026
  • Goldman Sachs has cut its end-2026 gold target to $4,150 from $4,650
  • The minutes of the Fed’s October meeting are the next catalyst

Gold fell below $3,800 an ounce in Asian trade on Wednesday, extending a slide to its lowest in more than a year as markets brace for a Federal Reserve rate hike next month. Spot gold dropped about 1.4% to around $3,795, after touching a low near $3,792, while futures fell almost 1.8%.

The driver is the same one that has dominated the past week: a Fed that is tightening rather than easing. Markets price roughly a 96% chance of a quarter-point hike in December, according to CME’s FedWatch tool, with a small chance of a half-point move. Fed Governor Christopher Waller added to those bets last week when he said a half-point hike may be needed if core inflation runs hot. US 10-year Treasury yields are hovering around 5.1%, and the dollar is near its strongest level in 19 months.

That combination works against gold on two fronts. Higher yields raise the opportunity cost of holding a metal that pays no income, and a stronger dollar makes it more expensive for buyers using other currencies.

The contrast with a year ago is stark. In November 2025, gold was beginning its climb to a record high as markets expected two or three Fed rate cuts in 2026. Twelve months on, the outlook has flipped from easing to tightening, and gold has given back a large part of those gains.

The Iran war has not provided the support many would expect. Rather than acting as a safe haven, gold has fallen as geopolitical risk has pushed up oil prices, which feeds into inflation, firms up Fed hike expectations and lifts yields. In this cycle, escalation in the Middle East has tended to hurt gold rather than help it.

Banks are adjusting their forecasts. Goldman Sachs analysts Lina Thomas and Daan Struyven have cut their end-2026 target to $4,150 an ounce from $4,650, arguing that a hawkish Fed could block the support gold usually gets from falling yields. Even the lower target implies a recovery of roughly 9% from current levels in a little over six weeks, which shows how quickly the outlook has shifted.

Attention now turns to the minutes of the Fed’s October meeting, due later on Wednesday in the US. A hawkish tone would reinforce December hike expectations and could push gold lower still, with some analysts watching support near $3,708. A softer message, or any sign that the Fed is uneasy about the recent sell-off in technology stocks, could give gold room to recover. For now, the market’s message is clear: as long as the Fed is hiking, gold is struggling to find buyers. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: TSMC reportedly demands cash up front from AI chip clients amid circular financing fears
item.description:
If confirmed, the move would be a vote of caution about AI customer finances from the company with the clearest view of chip demand. That would add weight to the circular financing debate that has hung over AI stocks this month. Custom chip designers and smaller AI players with stretched balance sheets would face tighter cash flow and could lose capacity to better-funded rivals. For TSMC, the policy would strengthen its pricing power and reduce its credit risk, a positive for the stock and for Taiwan’s tech-heavy market. Watch for any confirmation or denial from TSMC, which would set how seriously the report is taken.

---

While Nvidia extends credit to the AI boom, TSMC is reportedly asking its customers to show the money first, and that difference says a lot about who carries the risk.

Summary:

  • TSMC is reportedly setting credit limits for customers based on their balance sheets, payment history and default risk
  • Orders above the limit must reportedly be paid in cash, and some customers must prepay to secure capacity
  • The policy mainly affects custom AI chip makers, several of which are raising money through bonds, equity and loans
  • The report links the change to concerns about circular financing in AI
  • TSMC has not announced the policy, and the outlet could not confirm it independently

TSMC has begun weighing customers’ finances before handing out chipmaking capacity, setting credit limits and asking some buyers to pay cash up front, Chinese technology outlet Kuai Keji reported, citing industry sources. TSMC has not announced the policy, and the outlet said it could not independently confirm it. 

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co, or TSMC, is the world’s largest contract chipmaker. It does not design its own chips. Instead, it manufactures them for companies such as Nvidia, Apple, AMD and the growing number of firms building custom AI processors. Founded in Hsinchu in 1987, it produces the vast majority of the world’s most advanced chips. That gives it near-monopoly control of the capacity every AI company needs, and that leverage is what lets it set terms on who gets served first.

According to the report, TSMC now sets a credit limit for each customer based on its balance sheet. The assessment reportedly covers any history of late or unpaid bills, the customer’s standing in the industry, its business outlook and the estimated loss if it defaulted. Orders above that limit must be paid in cash, and some customers must prepay to secure their allocated capacity. The change is said to apply mainly to makers of custom AI chips, several of which are raising money through overseas convertible bonds, equity sales and syndicated bank loans.

The report links the shift directly to concerns about circular financing in the AI industry, where companies invest in one another and then buy from each other. In effect, TSMC would be moving from allocating capacity on a first-come, first-served basis to asking customers to prove they can pay.

That fits with comments from chief executive C.C. Wei, who has said on an earnings call that capacity planning takes into account cloud providers’ capital spending, their financial condition, and the availability of power and components. TSMC has also sent staff to the United States to check on data centre construction. The company already holds large customer prepayments, around NT$234 billion at the end of June, although Kuai Keji noted these are standard accounting prepayments rather than the new credit system.

The contrast with Nvidia is striking. Nvidia is increasingly acting as a financier of the AI build-out, with commitments of about $518 billion and customer receivables of about $81 billion, according to its latest results and a Financial Times report. TSMC, sitting further up the supply chain with near-monopoly control of advanced chipmaking, appears to be heading the other way, shifting risk back onto its customers.

If confirmed, the policy would tighten cash flow for chip designers that already tie up large sums in design and packaging costs, and it would favour well-funded customers over smaller players. It would also be a sign that the company best placed to judge AI demand wants protection in case some of its customers cannot pay. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Morgan Stanley sees USD/JPY fair value above 170, forecasts yen at 162 by late 2027
item.description:
A tier-one bank backing USD/JPY upside at these levels puts it in direct opposition to Japan’s Ministry of Finance, which has been warning about intervention near 160. That makes the pair asymmetric: it could grind higher on rate differentials, but intervention could drop it sharply in a single session. The Fed’s repricing is the main driver, so US data and Fed speakers matter more for USD/JPY than anything from Tokyo short of intervention. The short EUR vs AUD call gets support from today’s Australian wage beat, while the CHF leg leans on the franc’s safe-haven appeal while Middle East risks persist.

-

Morgan Stanley says a well-flagged December BOJ hike is no match for a Fed that is still tightening, and it is willing to bet against the yen right at Tokyo’s line in the sand.

Summary:

  • Morgan Stanley says long USD/JPY is its preferred trade on its fair value model, which it has put above 170
  • It sees room for further USD/JPY gains as markets reprice expectations for Fed rate hikes
  • Its strategists forecast the yen at 162 per dollar by Q4 2027, while Goldman Sachs takes the opposite view
  • The bank is staying short EUR against AUD and CHF
  • USD/JPY is trading near 160, where Tokyo has warned about intervention

Morgan Stanley says long USD/JPY remains its preferred trade based on its fair value model, and sees room for further gains as markets reprice the outlook for Federal Reserve rate hikes. The bank has estimated fair value for the pair above 170, well above the current level of around 159.5.

Its case rests on the yen’s sensitivity to global bond yields. Morgan Stanley has described the yen as the G10 currency most exposed to rising yields worldwide, and argues there is limited room for the Bank of Japan to surprise markets with a more hawkish move than is already expected. With US yields climbing on expectations that the Fed will keep tightening, that combination continues to favour the dollar against the yen.

The longer-term view points the same way. Morgan Stanley strategists including Serena Tang forecast the yen weakening to 162 per dollar by the fourth quarter of 2027. They argue that strong global risk appetite, Japan’s terms of trade and the continued appeal of carry trades will outweigh support from narrowing interest rate differentials. Goldman Sachs has taken the opposite view on the yen, a split that shows how hard the currency has become to call.

The bank is also staying short the euro against the Australian dollar and the Swiss franc. The Australian leg looks better supported after stronger than expected wage data on Wednesday added to the case for a hawkish Reserve Bank of Australia.

The main risk to the USD/JPY trade is Tokyo. The pair is trading just below 160, where Japanese officials have stepped up warnings about intervention, and MUFG expects action somewhere between here and 164, this year’s high. The last official intervention drove the pair from around 164 to 155 in under a week, a reminder of how quickly a crowded position can unwind.

The Bank of Japan is widely expected to raise its policy rate from 1.25% in December, and Governor Kazuo Ueda said on Wednesday that the bank will keep tightening. Morgan Stanley’s argument is that a well-flagged hike will not be enough to turn the yen while the Fed is also raising rates. For yen bulls, the turning point would need either a pause from the Fed or a much faster pace of tightening from Tokyo. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
